JUDGEMENT
PER HON’BLE MRS. SEEMA GUPTA, OFFICIATING CHAIRPERSON
1. The present Appeal has been filed by North East Transmission Company
Limited (“Appellant”) under Section 111 of the Electricity Act, 2003 challenging
the Order dated 27.01.2021 (“impugned order”) passed by Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred as “Central Commission/CERC”)
in Petition No.191/MP/2019, whereby the Central Commission rejected the
Appellant's claim for relaxation of the normative Operation and Maintenance
("O&M") expenses prescribed under the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2014.
Page 3 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
FACTUAL MATRIX OF THE CASE:
2. The Appellant-North East Transmission Company Limited ("NETCL") is a
transmission licensee incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act,
1956 and is engaged in the business of developing, operating and maintaining a
662.8 kms of inter-State transmission system for evacuation of power from the 2
x 363.3 MW Palatana Gas Based Power Project of ONGC Tripura Power
Company Limited (Respondent No. 10) in the North-Eastern Region. The system
comprises five transmission assets commissioned between 01.09.2012 and
22.02.2015.
Asset-I: Palatana–Silchar D/C, 247.39 km, COD 01.09.2012,
Asset-II: Silchar–Byrnihat, 214.41 km, COD 01.03.2013,
Asset-III: Byrnihat–Bongaigaon, 201 km, COD 22.02.2015,
Asset-IV: Silchar–Azara, 256.41 km, COD 27.07.2014, and
Asset-V: Azara–Bongaigaon, 159 km, COD 16.01.2015.
3. The Respondent No.1, i.e. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission is the
statutory body functioning under Section 76 of the Electricity Act, 2003. The
Respondent Nos. 2 to 11 are the concerned transmission utilities, distribution
utilities and other stakeholders/beneficiaries of the Appellant's transmission
system.
4. On 11.09.2015, NETCL filed Petition No. 233/TT/2015 before the CERC
seeking determination of tariff for Asset-I and Asset-II for the Control Period 2009-
14, which was decided by the CERC vide Order dated 29.07.2016. On the same
date, NETCL also filed Petition No. 213/TT/2015 seeking determination of tariff
Page 4 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
for Asset-I to Asset-V under the CERC Tariff Regulations, 2014, which was
subsequently determined by the CERC vide Order dated 16.08.2016.
5. Aggrieved by the inadequacy of the normative O&M expenses specified
under Regulation 29(4) of the Tariff Regulations, 2014, Appellant filed Petition No.
224/MP/2017 before the Central Commission under Regulations 54 and 55 of the
Tariff Regulations, 2014, seeking relaxation of the O&M norms applicable to its
transmission system, inter alia, on the ground that it is a single-project company
operating in the difficult terrain of the North-Eastern Region.
6. By Order dated 16.04.2019 in Petition No. 224/MP/2017, the Central
Commission observed that the Appellant, being a single asset company operating
in the North-Eastern Region, required consideration distinct from transmission
licensees having multiple assets. Accordingly, the Central Commission granted
liberty to the Appellant to file a fresh petition furnishing details regarding actual
O&M expenditure, efforts undertaken to optimize expenditure, and additional
costs incurred towards safety and security of the transmission assets.
7. On 04.07.2019,pursuant to the liberty granted by the Central Commission,
the Appellant filed Petition No. 191/MP/2019 before the Central Commission
providing details as sought under order dated 16.04.2019 and seeking exercise
of the power to relax under Regulation 54 of the Tariff Regulations, 2014, to give
appropriate O&M expenses commensurate with the actual requirements arising
from its unique operational circumstances.
8. By order dated 27.01.2021, CERC passed the order in Petition No.
191/MP/2019, and did not invoke provisions of power to relax to allow higher
Page 5 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
O&M charges to the Appellant for control period 2014-19. Aggrieved by the
rejection of its claim, the Appellant filed Review Petition No. 08/RP/2021 before
the Central Commission seeking review of the Order dated 27.01.2021 on the
ground that there existed errors apparent on the face of the record and that
relevant material facts had not been duly considered.
9. The Central Commission, by Order dated 06.08.2021, dismissed the
Review Petition at the admission stage, holding that the Appellant had failed to
demonstrate any error apparent on the face of the record warranting review of
the earlier order
10. Aggrieved by the Orders dated 27.01.2021 passed in Petition No.
191/MP/2019 and 06.08.2021 passed in Review Petition No. 08/RP/2021, the
Appellant has preferred the present Appeal.
ANALYSIS & DISCUSSION
11. Despite due service of notice, and matter having been listed on several
occasions, none appeared on behalf of the Respondents nor was vakalatnama
filed on behalf of any of the respondents. It appears that Respondents were not
keen to contest the present proceeding before this Tribunal. Accordingly, we
heard Ms. Poorva Saigal, learned counsel appearing for the Appellant, and
perused Impugned Order, written submission filed, and other documents on
record. Appellant has mainly contended that the i) impugned order contradicts
the central commission's own order dated 16.04.2019, ii) the normative O&M
benchmark is structurally inapplicable for a single project company in the North
Page 6 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
Eastern Region (NER), besides making other submissions on the observation
made against the Appellant in the Impugned Order.
12. The Appellant has relied upon the observation made by Central
Commission in its order dated 16.04.2019. The Relevant extract from CERC
Order dated 16.04.2019 passed in Petition No 224/MP/2017, seeking relaxation
in the O&M norms under Tariff Regulation 2014, for the control period 2014-19,
are reproduced below: :
“6. Considering the fact that the Petitioner is a single asset company and is
located in the North-Eastern Region, the Commission is of the view that the
case of the Petitioner needs to be considered differently from the transmission
assets of transmission licensees having multiple number of assets.
Accordingly, we grant liberty to the Petitioner to file a fresh petition containing
the following details:
(a) O&M charges paid for maintenance of the assets.
(b) O&M expenditure incurred by the Petitioner on items other than the
maintenance of the bays.
(c) Efforts made by the Petitioner to optimize the expenditure.
(d) Any additional expenditure incurred by the Petitioner on maintaining the
safety and security of the transmission assets.”
13. In pursuance of the liberty granted, Appellant filed the petition along with
the requisite particulars, culminating in the Impugned Order whereby relaxation
in O&M charges was declined. Upon careful scrutiny, we find substance in the
contention of the Appellant that the Impugned Order does not advert to or
deliberate upon the applicability of normative charges, derived on a pan-India
basis, to the peculiar circumstances of the Appellant, notwithstanding the
Commission’s earlier observation dated 16.04.2019 that special consideration
Page 7 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
may be warranted given the Appellant’s status as a single-project company
operating in the North-Eastern Region.
14. It is, however, trite law that a Regulatory Commission, being a statutory
authority, is not bound in perpetuity by every observation made in its earlier
orders, particularly where such observations are incidental or obiter dicta. The
binding force attaches to the operative directions and conclusions inter se the
parties, unless modified or set aside in appeal. Mere reasoning or incidental
remarks in one order do not create estoppel against the Commission in
subsequent proceedings.
15. Equally, it is well-settled that the judgments and observations of Regulatory
Commissions are not binding upon this Tribunal. The Tribunal’s remit under
Section 111 of the Electricity Act, 2003 is to test the legality, propriety, and
correctness of the impugned order on its own merits, in conformity with the parent
statute and applicable regulations. Accordingly, we shall proceed to decide the
issue on its own merit.
16. It is submitted that the data of Respondent No.2- POWERGRID,
substantially forms the basis of the normative benchmark, which operates
approximately 5,000 circuit kilometres of transmission lines in the North Eastern
Region as against its pan-India transmission network of over 1,53,635 circuit
kilometres, with the NER constituting merely 3.25% of its total network, which
was contended before CERC as well. Consequently, when POWERGRID’s O&M
expenses are aggregated at the national level to derive the normative per circuit
kilometre benchmark, the distinctly higher costs associated with the NER are
diluted within the national average. Appellant provided following data of

by 32 % to 127% as compared to other regions, normative benchmark of Rs.
0.403 lakh per circuit kilometre, derived from the national aggregate, is applied to

and hilly region and has applied a factor of 1.5 to the O&M expenses applied for
the other regions. It is, however, submitted that even with the application of 1.5

18. Appellant further submitted that while the Central Commission allowed
O&M expenses at the rate of Rs. 0.403 lakh per circuit kilometre, the
corresponding rates allowed for utilities operating in the North Eastern Region
were Rs. 0.85 lakh per circuit kilometre for AEGCL (Assam) and Rs. 1.09 lakh per
circuit kilometre for MEPTCL (Meghalaya). This clearly establishes that the State
Commissions regulated utilities operating under identical geographical, climatic
and operational conditions in the NER, including difficult terrain, high rainfall,
insurgency-related challenges and workforce constraints, for whom the O&M
norms were independently determined are approximately twice the normative
rates prescribed by the Central Commission.
19. In the Impugned Order, refuting the contention of Appellant, that Norms
were based only on POWERGRID O&M data, it is stated that norms are finalised
based on data collected for actual O&M expenses for all the transmission
licensee. Regarding the contention of Appellant with regard to higher O&M
charges being single project company, Impugned Order after noting the
Page 10 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
Statement of reasons to CERC Tariff Regulation 2014, that such aspect has been
clearly deliberated, following observations is made.
“25. It is observed from the above that the issue of single project companies
and associated expenditure has been raised while finalizing norms for O&M
Expenses during 2009-14 as well as 2014-19 tariff periods. However, the
Commission has not agreed to such suggestions of allowing higher O&M
Expenses and has been of the view that single project companies need to
undertake more efficient measures to contain the O&M expenses within
industry benchmarks.”
20. Though, it may generally be true that single project company, may not enjoy
the economies of scale as other licensee with multiple project, however it is
observed from the record that while finalising the Tariff Regulations, 2014, the
Central Commission undertook detailed deliberation and consideration of the
suggestions advanced by stakeholders, including the plea for a differentiated
methodology or higher normative O&M charges for single-project companies. The
Central Commission, however, consciously decided not to introduce
differentiation on the basis of the number of projects operated by a company.
Instead, the normative framework was anchored on circuit-kilometre (ckt-km)
parameters, which were considered to be a more objective and uniform basis for
determination of O&M charges across the sector for the period under
consideration. Once such Regulations are notified under Section 178/181 of the
Electricity Act, 2003, they acquire the force of subordinate legislation and are
binding upon the Commission itself, the licensees, and all stakeholders, until
modified or struck down by a competent judicial authority. Any departure from
the normative framework prescribed in the Regulations must be justified strictly
within the contours of the enabling provisions, and not on the basis of mere
observations in prior orders.
Page 11 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
21. With regard to statement in the Impugned Order that O&M norms under
tariff Regulation 2014 were based on data of all the Transmission Licensees and
not on POWERGRID alone, we find that it is not discernible from the Impugned
Order that what other transmission licensee data was considered while forming
the norms for FY 2014-19 and percentage share of asset base of these
transmission licensee in the overall inter- State transmission network asset base
operating prior to 2014-19 control period. It is not difficult to reach to the
conclusion as also submitted by Appellant, that no operational data could have
been provided by the Appellant at the time of finalization of the Tariff Regulations,
2014, because the assets had not been commissioned by that time. Equally, we
cannot be oblivious to the fact that prior to Control period 2014-19, POWERGRID,
as the inter-state transmission licensee was operating major portion of the inter-
State Transmission network. In such circumstances, it can be easily assumed
that the overall O&M charges of POWERGRID for the control period prior to 2014-
19 would have had a controlling impact and constituted contributing factor in
arriving at benchmark or normative O&M data for control Period 2014-19.
22. It is observed from the CERC Tariff Regulation 2014, that the normative
operation and maintenance expenses were same Pan India, with no
differentiation for the different terrain i.e, plain, hilly, snowy, difficult etc. In the
Tariff Regulation 2014, the normative O&M charges for substation, is bay wise
based on voltage level whether 765 kV /400 kV /220 kv and so on; higher the
voltage- higher the O&M charges and for transmission lines it is on the basis of
number of conductors used in single circuit or double circuit ; more the number
of conductors – more O&M charges.
Page 12 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
23. Further, from the region-wise POWERGRID data submitted by Appellant
and as noted above, it is evident that the O&M cost per circuit kilometer varies
significantly between different regions, which in our view is primarily attributable
to the type of terrain and topography involved. The data clearly indicates that the
O&M charges per kilometer of transmission line are highest for the North Eastern
Region as compared to other regions. Specifically, the O&M cost per circuit
kilometer in the North Eastern Region (Rs. 0.75 lakh) is 127% higher than the
Western Region, 32% higher than the Northern Region, and 79% higher than the
Southern Region. For a transmission licensee operating on a pan-India basis,
such aberrations in regional O&M costs can be mitigated when evaluated at the
company level, even if uniform normative O&M charges are applied across
regions. However, the same mitigation is not feasible for a licensee whose
operations are confined solely to the North Eastern Region, such as the
Appellant. In such a case, the application of pan-India normative O&M charges,
without relaxation, may result in inequitable treatment and compromise
operational sustainability, given the demonstrably higher costs inherent to the
region’s terrain and topology.
24. Further, the Impugned Order records an observation that the “However, the
Petitioner had failed to submit data regarding O&M expenses while the Central
Commission was engaged in formulating the norms for the control period
2019-24. It is not correct on the part of the Petitioner to suggest that the norms
were finalised based on data of PGCIL only.” This assertion has been strongly
refuted by the Appellant. Upon careful scrutiny, we find substance in the
submissions advanced.
25. From the records placed before us, it appears that the Appellant did, in fact,
submit detailed operational and financial data on 24.01.2019 in response to the
Page 13 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
Central Commission’s Public Notice dated 10.11.2017, which had invited
stakeholder comments on the Draft Tariff Regulations, 2019 for the control period
2019-24. The submission of such data evidences the Appellant’s participation in
the consultative process and contradicts the Commission’s finding that no data
was furnished. We have observed some variation between the data submitted by
the Appellant on 24.01.2019 and the audited data subsequently filed in Petition
No. 191/MP/2019. However, the existence of such variation does not negate the
fact of submission itself.
26. In these circumstances, the observation in the Impugned Order that no data
was submitted by the Appellant for finalising the O&M norms for the control period
2019-24 is contrary to the record and cannot be sustained. The Commission’s
finding on this aspect is accordingly set aside.
27. Appellant has contended the observations in Para 31 of the Impugned
Order, that Appellant was aware of the applicable O&M norms under tariff
regulation and incurring expenditure on both site offices and corporate functions
is not a prudent expenditure, being erroneous in law and on facts. It is submitted
that the expenditure incurred on site offices was unavoidable, as the scope of
the O&M Agreement with POWERGRID specifically excluded several critical
activities, including maintenance of terminal bays, hot-line maintenance, payment
of forest lease rent, liaison with Government authorities, procurement of spares,
payment of crop/tree compensation within the Right of Way corridor, and
emergency coordination with the RLDC; and accordingly these functions
necessarily required dedicated on-site personnel and could not have been
effectively discharged through remote administration. Further, after the O&M
agreement entered between the Appellant and POWERGRID came to an end on
31.07.2021, O&M activities have been carried out by the Appellant itself. The
Page 14 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
maintenance of site offices was therefore not a permanent overhead but an
interim operational necessity during the transition to in-house O&M. This was
specifically placed before the Central Commission but has not been considered
in the Impugned Order. Appellant placed reliance on the Judgment dated
04.05.2026 passed by this Tribunal in “M/s Everest Power Pvt. Ltd. v. Punjab
State Electricity Regulatory Commission” Appeal No. 430 of 2019, to contend
that prudence review must be undertaken with reference to the necessity and
reasonableness of the expenditure in the facts and circumstances of the case.
With regard to high corporate expenses, as observed in the Impugned Order, it
is submitted that the entire corporate expenses of Appellant were divided into
limited number of assets/ single project resulting in higher percentage when
compared with other transmission licensee like POWERGRID which has over 400
assets spread across five regions.
28. Our attention has been drawn to the fact that Central Commission has
subsequently taken cognizance of the difficulties being faced by the Licensees
operating in the NER and hilly region and has applied a factor of 1.5 to the O&M
expenses applied for the other regions and the relevant extracts from the
Explanatory Memorandum to the Draft Tariff Regulations, 2024 reads as under:
Approval of O&M Expenses for North East/Hilly Regions
16.5.23 The Commission, with regard to whether additional O&M expenses
can be given for transmission assets being operated in the North Eastern and
Hilly Regions, based on the actual data submitted, observes that the actual
expenses incurred in the NER region are higher than compared to other
regions and therefore, the Commission acknowledges the elevated costs
associated with transmission projects in hilly terrains. Factors such as
increased logistic, erection, labour, and transportation costs contribute to
higher O&M expenses in these regions compared to mainland projects. The
Commission, therefore, proposes to allow O&M expenses by applying a factor
of 1.5 to the O&M expenses determined under Regulation 36. As the O&M
norms have been worked out considering the actual O&M expenses of all the
regions of PGCIL which includes NE, NER and other hilly regions, therefore
Page 15 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
it is clarified that the factor of 1.50 shall be applicable only to those
transmission licensees whose transmission assets are located solely in NE
Region, States of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh, the Union Territories
of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
29. The 1.5 factor has been incorporated as a Proviso to Regulation 36(3) of
the Tariff Regulations, 2024 as noted under:
“Provided further that the O&M expenses for Transmission Licensees whose
transmission assets are located solely in NE Regions, State of Uttarakhand
and Himachal Pradesh, the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and
Ladakh shall be worked out by multiplying 1.50 to the normative O&M
expenses prescribed above”.
From the above, it is clear that CERC, appreciating the difficulties faced by
Transmission Licensee in O&M of transmission Assets solely operating in NER
and/or other hilly regions, and involving additional expenditure, a multiplication
factor of 1.5 to the normative O&M has been adopted for such licensees in Tariff
Regulation 2024.
30. We take cognizance of the fact that the transmission corridor operated by
the Appellant is critical for evacuation of power in the North-Eastern Region and
caters to approximately one-third of the power demand of the region, as recorded
in CERC order dated 16.04.2019. It is submitted on behalf of Appellant that it
consistently maintained a transmission system availability in excess of 99.90%,
with an average availability of approximately 99.92% during the relevant tariff
period, despite operating in difficult geographical conditions characterized by hilly
terrain, heavy rainfall, forest areas, river crossings and insurgency-related
challenges.
31. Appellant has made specific contention with regard to Section 5.11(h)(2) of
the Tariff Policy, 2016 – ‘Multi Year Tariff’ which provides as under:

"In cases where operations have been much below the norms for many
previous years, the initial starting point in determining the revenue
requirement and the improvement trajectories should be recognized at
'relaxed' levels and not the 'desired' levels. Suitable benchmarking
studies may be conducted to establish the 'desired' performance
standards."
Further, the Section 61 of the Electricity Act, 2003 requires that the Appropriate
Commission, while determining terms and conditions for tariff, shall be guided by
principles that safeguard the consumer's interest and ensure recovery of cost of
electricity in a reasonable manner.

33. Admittedly, the O&M expenditure incurred by Appellant for the Control
Period FY 2014-19 were considerably higher, more than double, as compared to
what is allowed to them applying Normative O&M charges for the period. While
turning down the request of Appellant for relaxation in the O&M norms, it is
observed that Commission expects the Petitioner to be more prudent and restricts
its O&M charges within the stipulated norms.
34. It is axiomatic that the Regulatory Commissions, while discharging their
statutory functions, must emphasise efficiency improvement and safeguard
consumer interest. The underlying normative framework is designed to balance
cost recovery with efficiency gains, thereby ensuring that consumer interest is
protected while simultaneously allowing a reasonable return to the licensee.
However, it cannot be gainsaid that every element of extra expenditure incurred
by a utility can be curtailed by efficiency improvement. Equally, relaxation cannot
be granted merely on the basis of actual higher expenditure unless such
expenditure is demonstrably linked to prudence and necessity. A balanced
approach, therefore, requires the Commission to weigh both sides of the
equation. In circumstances where a licensee operates under peculiar
conditions—such as geographical remoteness or region-specific challenges—the
Commission must deliberate whether strict adherence to pan-India norms would
result in inequitable treatment, compromise operational sustainability, or vitiate
the licensee’s viability.
35. Regulation 54 of the Tariff Regulations, 2014 confers upon the Central
Commission the enabling power to relax any provision of the Regulations in
exceptional circumstances, subject to the requirement that reasons for such
relaxation be recorded in writing. This relaxation power is not to be exercised
lightly or in routine manner, but only where the factual matrix discloses
Page 18 of 20

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 296 of 2021
circumstances of such peculiar nature that strict adherence to the regulatory norm
would result in manifest hardship or inequity. The Electricity Act, 2003, while
mandating the Commission to safeguard the interests of consumers,
simultaneously obliges it to ensure that the cost of electricity is recovered in a
reasonable manner, thereby striking a balance between consumer protection and
viability of regulated entities.
36. In the present case, the Appellant’s operations are confined exclusively to
the North Eastern Region, as also observed by CERC in its earlier order, which
is characterised by hilly terrain, difficult accessibility, and operational challenges
not ordinarily encountered in other regions. The peculiar geographical and
logistical constraints faced by the Appellant, coupled with the fact that it is solely
operating in North Eastern Region, constitute exceptional circumstances within
the meaning of Regulation 54. To insist upon a rigid application of the normative
O&M charges in such a situation would be inequitable and contrary to the
statutory mandate of ensuring reasonable recovery of costs. We accordingly find
merit in the submissions advanced by the Appellant and hold that the case
warrants favourable consideration for relaxation in the norms of O&M charges for
the control period under consideration.
CONCLUSION
37. In view of the foregoing deliberations, the Impugned Order is set aside.
The matter is remanded to the Central Commission with a specific direction to
exercise its power to relax under Regulation 54 of the Tariff Regulations, 2014,
for the limited purpose of working out the O&M charges for the assets of the

ISSUE I: DIRECTION TO REFUND FIXED COSTS FOR PLANTS LESS THAN
10 YEARS.
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF APPELLANT
5. It is submitted that State Commission has wrongly calculated recoverable
capacity charge for RGTPP and DCRTPP for FY 2014-15. The Regulation
30(c)(i) of the MYT Regulations, 2012 prescribes a specific and distinct formula
for recovery of annual fixed charges for generating stations in commercial
operation for less than ten (10) years on 1st April of the financial year, which has
been overlooked by the State Commission. In terms of these Regulations,
DCRTPP (COD: 24.06.2008) and RGTPP (COD: 01.03.2011) shall fall in this
category.
The formula prescribed in MYT Regulations 2012 is identical in substance to
Regulation 21(2) of the Central Commission's Tariff Regulations, 2009, which was
consistently applied by the Central Commission during that period. The
Statement of Reasons issued by CERC for the 2009 Tariff Regulations dated
03.02.2009 expressly recognizes the distinction between younger and older
stations and is consciously conceived to balance incentives and disincentives
based on the stage of operational life of a plant.
Page 4 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
6. The Appellant submits that State Commission has also misconstrued the
term "pro-rata". As clarified in the Statement of Reasons, "pro-rata" does not
imply strict linear proportionality, rather it denotes variation in proportion to
another variable. Regulation 30(c)(i) fully satisfies this requirement, as capacity
charges vary proportionately with monthly availability. The interpretation of “pro
rata” which results in a conflict with another Regulation is contrary to the settled
principle of interpretation that both provisions need to be harmoniously construed.
It cannot be that a provision in a particular statute is termed as bad as there is a
conflict with another provision in the very same statute.
7. State Commission's finding that Regulation 30(c)(i) is merely a monthly
computation mechanism, and yearly capacity charges would be recovered as per
Regulation 30 (a), is contrary to the plain language of Regulation 30(c)(i), which
expressly provides for annual correction through its proviso. The contention of
respondents that the plant with zero annual PAF would recover 50% of AFC under
Regulation 30 (c), is factually and mathematically incorrect as with PAFY= 0, the
proviso yields zero recovery, thus there is no conflict with Regulation 30(a). The
Appellant further contends that The State Commission's characterization of
Regulation 30(c)(i) as an 'aberration' is legally untenable and contrary to
established principles of statutory construction. Regulation 30(c)(i) constitutes a
special provision governing the computation of AFC for generating stations that
are less than ten years old and, therefore, in accordance with the settled principle
that a special provision prevails over a general provision.
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF RESPONDENT No 2- HPPC
8. It is submitted that Regulation 30(a) is the governing provision for
determination of annual fixed charge recovery for all thermal generating stations,
Page 5 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
irrespective of their age or date of commissioning. Regulation 30(c)(i), on the
other hand, is a monthly computation mechanism that uses the notations “for a
calendar month”, making it plain that it governs only monthly payments. The State
Commission has therefore, correctly applied Regulation 30(a) for the annual
determination and is right in holding that Regulation 30(c)(i) operates only as the
monthly billing mechanism.
9. HPPC further submits that the Appellant's interpretation of Regulation
30(c)(i) is contrary to Regulations 30(a) and proviso in 30(c)(i). HPPC submits
that if PAFM is 100% every month and then the availability factor would be
0.5+0.5 x (100/85) = 0.5+0.5x 1.1765 +0.5+0.5882 = 1.0882. The above
cumulatively would give a much higher capacity charge recovery then what would
be admissible at 85% availability prescribed in Regulation 30(a) i.e. 0.5+0.5 x
(85/85) = 0.5+0.5x 1.1765 + 0.5+0.5882 = 1.
Further, the formula in Regulation 30(c)(i) also conflicts with the proviso to
Regulation 30(c)(i) at zero availability: while the proviso rightly yields zero
recovery, the main formula would yield 50% recovery at zero availability.
Harmonious construction requires reading Regulation 30(c)(i) to be confined to
monthly mechanism only and cannot be applied to annual determination.
10. In any event, notwithstanding the amounts paid during individual month, at
the end of financial year, the fixed charges are adjusted to the extent of PLF
actually achieved i.e. to the extent of 78% for DCRTPP and 76.34 % for RGTPP
1-2 as indicated in the appeal.
11. Reliance has been placed on the settled principle that literal interpretation
cannot be employed where it leads to absurdity or inconsistency as held in
Page 6 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
[Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India, (2006) 7 SCC 1. Departure from literal
interpretation is permissible only where the natural meaning leads to repugnance,
inconsistency, or absurdity. [Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Admn.), (1988) 3 SCC
609, (Paras 231-232, 238-239); Maulavi Hussein Haji Abraham Umarji v. State
of Gujarat, (2004) 6 SCC 672.
12. HPPC further submits that Regulations 80 and 81 of the MYT Regulations,
2012 empower the State Commission to interpret the Regulations and adopt an
appropriate procedure to safeguard consumer interest.
OUR CONSIDERATION
13. The central issue for adjudication is whether recovery of Annual Fixed
Charges for the generating stations DCRTPP and RGTPS Units 1 & 2, which had
completed less than ten years of commercial operation as on 1st April 2014,
ought to be governed by Regulation 30(c)(i) or Regulation 30(a) of the MYT
Regulations, 2012. The Appellant has urged that Regulation 30(c)(i) is a specific
provision enacted to deal with plants within ten years of commercial operation,
and therefore the computation of fixed charges must be made strictly in terms
thereof. It is not disputed that for FY 2014-15, DCRTPP achieved an annual
availability of 78.00% and RGTPS Units 1 & 2 achieved 76.34% against the
prescribed normative annual availability of 85%.
14. In the Impugned Order dated 31.03.2016, annual fixed charges have been
worked out on prorate basis in terms of Regulation 30 (a) considering actual
availability less than NAPAF. In the Impugned review order dated 29.06.2016,
after extracting the entire Regulation 30, it has been held that it is the Regulation
Page 7 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
30 (a) which governs recovery of annual charges for these plants. It has been
further held that the “Proviso of Regulation 30 (c)i is a non obstante clause and
cannot be read harmoniously with Regulation 30 (a) because with annual PLF
zero, a thermal plant less than 10 years old will get 50 % annual fixed charges as
per said proviso to Regulation 30 (c)(i), whereas as per Regulation 30 (a) it is
entitled to get zero capacity charge. So there is an aberration in Regulation 30
(c)(i) and this aberration has come to the notice of commission only now and shall
be addressed while framing/ notifying MYT regulations for the next control
period”….. .
15. It is relevant to extract the applicable provisions of the Haryana Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Multi Year Tariff) Regulations, 2012 ("MYT Regulations,
2012"), which govern the issues arising in the present Appeal. The relevant
Regulations are reproduced hereunder for ready reference:
30 RECOVERY OF ANNUAL FIXED CHARGES (CAPACITY) CHARGES FOR
THERMAL POWER PROJECTS
(a) A generating plant shall recover full capacity charge at the normative annual plant
availability factor specified for it by the Commission. Recovery of capacity charge
below the level of target availability shall be on pro-rata basis. No capacity charge
shall be payable at zero availability;
(b) Payment of capacity charge by the beneficiaries shall be on monthly basis in
proportion to allocated / contracted capacity. The total capacity charges payable
for a generating plant shall be shared by its beneficiaries as per their respective
percentage share / allocation in the capacity of the generating plant;
(c) The capacity charge payable to a thermal generating plant (in Rs.) for a calendar
month shall be calculated in accordance with the following formula:
(i) Generating plants in commercial operation for less than ten (10) years on 1st
April of the financial year:
AFC x (NDM / NDY) x (0.5 + 0.5 x PAFM / NAPAF)

(PAFY) is less than 70%, the total capacity charge for the year shall be restricted
to
AFC x (0.5+ 35/NAPAF) x (PAFY/70)
(ii) For generating plants in commercial operation for ten (10) years or more on
1st April of the financial year:

Where,
AFC = Annual fixed cost specified for the year, in Rupees.
NAPAF = Cumulative Normative annual plant availability factor in percentage
NDM = Number of days in the month
NDY = Number of days in the year
PAFM = Plant availability factor achieved during the month, in percent:
PAFY = Plant availability factor achieved during the year, in percent
Note: Until Intra - State ABT is implemented, Plant Availability Factor (PAF), wherever
mentioned, shall mean Plant Load Factor (PLF). For working out annual PLF for the
purpose of recovery of annual fixed charges, deemed generation on account of backing
down on the instructions of SLDC or on the request of Discoms shall be included.”
16. From the perusal of Regulation 30, it is evident that for plants which have
completed less than 10 years of commercial operation, there is a special
category for calculation of monthly fixed charges under Regulation 30 (c)(i) and
its proviso deals with capping of annual fixed charges in case availability achieved
is less than 70 %.
17. We therefore, find considerable merit in the submission of the Appellant.
Regulation 30(c)(i), read with its proviso, is not confined to a monthly computation
mechanism but expressly contemplates annual correction based on the Plant
Availability Factor for the year (PAFY). The respondents’ contention as well as
observations in the Impugned Review Order that a generating station with zero
annual PAF would yet recover fifty percent of the Annual Fixed Charges (AFC)
Page 9 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
under Regulation 30(c) is factually and mathematically unsustainable, for the
proviso yields zero recovery when PAFY equals zero and as such proviso
becomes applicable as soon as PAFY falls below 70 %. Thus, there is no
inconsistency with Regulation 30(a).
-
18. Regulation 30(c)(i) constitutes a special provision applicable to generating
stations less than ten years old. The legal maxim, generalia specialibus non
derogant, is squarely applicable; each enactment must be construed in that
respect according to its own subject-matter and its own terms. special provision
prevails over a general one as per the settled statutory construction, (South India
Corporation v. Secretary, Board of Revenue, AIR 1964 SC 207; J.K. Cotton
Spinning & Weaving Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of U.P., AIR 1961 SC 1170). This
principle has also been applied to resolve any conflict between general and
special provisions in the same legislative instrument, and it has been held that in
case of conflict, between a special provision and a general provision, the special
provision prevails over the general provision, and the general provision applies
to such cases which are not covered by the special provision. (Kureti
Venkateswarlu, President v. State of Andhra Pradesh, 1970 SCC OnLine AP
33).
19. It is well settled that where a statute provides for a thing to be done in a
particular manner, then it has to be done in that manner, and in no other manner
[ Chandra Kishore Jha v. Mahavir Prasad [(1999) 8 SCC 266 : AIR 1999 SC
3558] (SCC para 17 : AIR para 12), Dhanajaya Reddy v. State of Karnataka
[(2001) 4 SCC 9 : 2001 SCC (Cri) 652 : AIR 2001 SC 1512] (SCC para 23 : AIR
para 22), NTPC Ltd. v. CERC & Ors. (Judgment in Appeal No. 125 of 2017
Page 10 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
dated 09.05.2019), NTPC Ltd v. CERC & Ors. (Order in Appeal No 93 of 2017
dated 29.01.2020]. Therefore, the general statute is read as silently excluding
from its operation the cases which have been provided for by the Special one.
(Maxwel on the Interpretation of Statutes, Eleventh Edition, page 168). In the
present case, the Commission’s characterization of Regulation 30(c)(i) as an
‘aberration’ is legally untenable, for no provision of delegated legislation can be
treated as surplusage unless irreconcilable, and courts are bound to give effect
to every word of the statute (Aswini Kumar Ghose v. Arabinda Bose, AIR 1952
SC 369).
20. We are therefore, of the view that Regulation 30(c)(i) governs the
computation of AFC for such stations which are operating for less than 10 years
from its commercial operation date , and its operation cannot be diluted by resort
to Regulation 30(a). In addition, it has been brought to our notice that Regulation
30(c)(i) of the MYT Regulations, 2012, is identical to Regulation 21(2) of the
Central Commission’s Tariff Regulations, 2009, a fact not disputed by
Respondents, and same has been consistently applied by the Central
Commission during that period. The Statement of Reasons issued by the Central
Commission for the 2009 Tariff Regulations issued on 03.02.2009, explains the
rationale for prescribing different incentive/disincentive structures for stations
younger than 10 years and those older than 10 years as noted hereunder:
“………………………………….
25.19 With regard to incentive/disincentive rate to be adopted, we are of the
view that following aspects are important in this regard:
If the disincentive could be in the form of denial of normative fixed charge for
availability lower than the normative then the incentive could be in the form of
additional fixed charge for availability in higher than the normative.
As such, recovery of fixed charge shall be on monthly basis and shall be
inclusive of any incentive and disincentive depending upon the availability
Page 11 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
achieved during the month. This is a departure from the earlier practice of
recovery of fixed charges linked to cumulative availability. This would allow
the beneficiaries to meet any shortfall in availability (due to station being out
partially or full) be met from sourcing supplies from alternate sources or over
drawal from the grid at UI rates.
It would be easier for the new generating station to achieve the availability
above normative whereas as the station become old it would be more credit
worthy for the station to achieve availability above the normative. As such,
rate of incentive should be more for stations which are in operation for more
than 10 year from the COD in terms of normative fixed charge as compared
to new stations which are in operation for 10 year or less from the COD.
The incentive and disincentive should be symmetrical in the normal operating
range. For a thermal generating station normal operating range could be
considered as station availability of 70% and above. However, availability of
less than 70% should not be acceptable and should be accompanied with
denial of fixed charges on pro-rata basis. Since the recovery of fixed charges
is based on monthly availability actual picture would become clear only at the
end of the year and hence correction of incentive at the end of year in case
annual availability achieved is lower than 70% is being allowed.”

23. It is evident from the above mathematical computation that in both
scenarios—Scenario A (plants less than ten years old under Regulation 30(c)(i))
and Scenario B (plants beyond ten years under Regulation 30(a) or 30(c)(ii))—
the annual fixed cost remains the same for the achieved availability of 85%.
Under Scenario A, the disincentive in AFC recovery below 70% availability is
moderated, and the incentive above normative availability is also correspondingly
limited. The proviso to Regulation 30(c)(i) expressly caps recovery when
availability falls below 70%, thereby ensuring consumer protection while allowing
moderated recovery for newer plants.
24. In contrast, under Scenario B, for plants beyond ten years of commercial
operation, the incentive and disincentive are sharper, whether computed under
Regulation 30(c)(ii) or Regulation 30(a) on a pro-rata basis. This differentiation is
deliberate, reflecting the rationale articulated in the Statement of Objects and
Reasons to the CERC Tariff Regulations, 2009, which recognized the need to
balance recovery for newer plants against consumer interest.
25. We also do not find any merit in the contention of the respondents that the
Appellant’s interpretation of Regulation 30(c)(i) is contrary to Regulation 30(a)
and its proviso, merely because if PAFM were 100% every month, the availability
factor would mathematically yield 1.0882 as compared to the normative 85%
availability prescribed in Regulation 30(a). It is evident from above mathematical
Page 15 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
calculations for NAFM 90 %, that the calculation of annualised fixed charges
yield different incentives for the same NAFM for plants with less than 10 years of
commercial operation and more than 10 years of commercial operation, and
same can be extrapolated for NAFM of 100 %, which squarely fits into the rational
explained in the Statement of Reasons as noted above. As per Regulation 30 (a),
the generating company shall recover full capacity charge at Normative Plant
Availability factor, which is found to be same under both the scenarios as per
Regulation 30 (c) also, as noted above. As per applicable regulatory scheme,
for plants with less than 10 years of commercial operation, separate formula has
been given for computation of monthly and annual fixed capacity charges and in
case annual availability falls below 70 %, the annual fixed charges gets capped
as per formula prescribed under the proviso of Regulation 30(c) (i). As such,
computational anomalies, if any, cannot override the express text of a special
provision, nor justify its displacement by a general clause. The correct interpretive
approach is to give effect to Regulation 30(c)(i) in its entirety, harmonizing it with
the broader scheme, rather than nullifying it under the guise of anomaly.
26. We therefore hold that Regulation 30(c)(i) constitutes a specific provision
for generating stations with less than ten years of commercial operation, and its
operation must be harmonized with Regulation 30(a) and 30(c)(ii). One provision
of the regulation cannot be construed to render another otiose; each must be
given effect in its proper sphere. The mathematical scheme corroborates the
regulatory intent, and the differentiation between younger and older plants is
rational, consistent with the objectives of the Tariff Regulations.

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
27. Since the underlying principles were consciously adopted and replicated in
the State Commission’s MYT Regulations, 2012 in Regulation 30(c)(i), the
Commission cannot, under the guise of interpretation, rewrite the regulation.
Moreover no aberration in Regulation 30(c)(i) has been demonstrated as noted
in the Impugned Review Order . The reliance placed by the respondents on
Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India, (2006) 7 SCC 1 (para 201); Kehar Singh v.
State (Delhi Admn.), (1988) 3 SCC 609 (paras 231–232, 238–239); and
Maulavi Hussein Haji Abraham Umarji v. State of Gujarat, (2004) 6 SCC 672
(paras 21–23) is misplaced, as those authorities pertain to constitutional
interpretation and legislative intent, whereas the present case involves the
construction of specific tariff regulations where the text and scheme are clear.
28. In view of the foregoing deliberations, the findings in the Impugned Order
that annual fixed charges are to be calculated as per Regulation 30(a) for RGTPP
Units 1 & 2 and DCRTPP, which have not completed ten years of commercial
operation, are set aside. It is held that monthly and annual fixed charges for these
plants shall be calculated in terms of Regulation 30(c)(i). The matter is
accordingly remanded to the State Commission to work out the annual fixed
charges in the above terms.
ISSUE II: TRUING-UP OF FIXED COSTS WITHOUT CONSIDERING FORCE
MAJEURE CONDITIONS.
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF APPELLANT
29. Appellant submits that RGTPP Unit-II remained unavailable from October
2013 to June 2014 due to a turbine failure. The OEM (SEC Ltd., China) required
the machine to be transported to China for repairs, resulting in an unavoidable
outage that squarely falls within the Regulation 3.23(vi) of the MYT Regulations,
Page 17 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
2012, which recognizes shutdowns required to avoid serious and immediate risk
of equipment failure as force majeure. The State Commission, by its Order dated
27.03.2015 passed in the True-up for FY 2013-14, had expressly acknowledged
that the station faced significant operational constraints beyond the control of the
Appellant and that the Appellant made earnest and bona fide efforts to mitigate
the issues. The Appellant contends that the subsequent reversal of this finding,
as recorded in the impugned order, without fresh material is arbitrary and violates
the doctrine of legitimate expectation and principles of regulatory consistency.
30. Appellant submits that the State Commission, with respect to WYC Hydel,
in the Order dated 27.03.2015, acknowledged the technical incapacity and force-
majeure type limitation affecting the station and had relaxed the normative PLF
to 50% of available capacity (46.4 MW) for FY 2015-16. This recognition of the
inherent limitations of the WYC Hydel machines (which have outlived their
designed life) should equally apply to the computation of fixed charges for FY
2014-15.
31. The Appellant submits that although the Regulations do not specifically
provide for PLF relaxation in respect of foreign-manufactured equipment, the
MYT framework empowers the State Commission to grant relaxation where
performance shortfalls arise from uncontrollable factors such as OEM-related
failures, non-availability of spares, or specialized repair requirements.
32. With regard to Respondent’s contention that order dated 27.03.2015
attained finality because it was not challenged is legally untenable. The mere
absence of an appeal does not convert an incorrect finding into a correct one. It
is settled law that an erroneous order cannot attain legality solely by remaining
unchallenged. Legality of order must be tested on its merit.
Page 18 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
SUBMISSIONS URGED ON BEHALF OF RESPONDENT No 2- HPPC
33. It is submitted that Plant Load Factor / Plant Availability Factor is expressly
classified as a 'controllable item' under Regulation 8.3(b) of the MYT Regulations,
2012, therefore, such equipment breakdown does not fall under force majeure
and loss incurred by the same cannot be passed on to the Discoms and
consumers of Haryana.
34. RGTPP Unit-2 suffered from inherent turbine problems since
commissioning. A mechanical failure arising from inherent design deficiencies or
maintenance lapses cannot constitute 'force majeure' under Regulation 3.23, as
noted in multiple prior orders (including Order dated 13.10.2014 in Case No.
HERC/PRO-13 of 2014 and the Order dated 29.05.2014 in Case No. 39 of 2013).
35. It is submitted that Appellant has misconstrued the nature and scope of the
finding in the Order dated 27.03.2015 as the said order dealt with HPGCL's
petition for True-up for FY 2013-14, and Tariff Determination for FY 2015-16 in
which State Commission noted that HPGCL made earnest efforts to bring back
the machine in service, the State Commission, however, did not relax the PLF for
FY 2014-15.
36. With regard to WYC Hydel, the State Commission has noted that the WYC
Hydel machine have outlived their useful life and the efficiency has gone down
considerably and while noting that HPGCL has not taken timely actions for
maintenance, the State Commission determined the PLF at 50% for WYC Hydel
for FY 2015-16. These observations did not amount to a general relaxation of
fixed charge recovery norms or grant any relief from refund of excess fixed
charges for FY 2013-14 or FY 2014-15.
Page 19 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
37. The State Commission in the Review Order has held that in regard to the
RGTPS Units no relaxation can be granted in the normative PLF as far as
recovery of fixed charges is concerned". It has been further clarified that a
relaxed PLF of 70% had been approved for RGTPP in FY 2013-14 " for the limited
purpose of working out target generation and fuel cost" by relying on the
Generation Tariff Order dated 29.03.2013 for FY 2013-14 Furthermore, in the
same order dated 29.03.2013, the State Commission had stated that "non-
availability of a generating station for a prolonged period imposes significant cost
on the electricity consumers of Haryana in terms of loss of productivity or
substituting the same with short term expensive power or prohibitively expensive
CPP running on liquid fuel.
38. It is further submitted that the Appellant had separately filed Case No.
HERC/PRO-13 of 2014 seeking recovery of fixed charges for shutdown of
RGTPP Unit-2 and recovery at actual PLF for FY 2014-15, which was rejected by
the State Commission vide Order dated 13.10.2014 (in Petition 39 of 2013) and
same has been reproduced in the Review Order.
CONSIDERATION AND OUR VIEW
39. The issue involved is with regard to relaxation in the plant availability factor
for RGTPP Unit-II, which remained unavailable from October 2013 to June 2014
due to a turbine failure for the year under consideration i.e. FY 2014-15,
especially when State Commission in its order dated 27.03.2015 passed in the
True-up for FY 2013-14, had expressly acknowledged that the station faced
significant operational constraints beyond the control of the Appellant and that the
Appellant made earnest and bona fide efforts to mitigate the issues. It has been
Page 20 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
contended on behalf of Appellant that Regulation 3.23(vi) of the MYT Regulations,
2012, recognizes shutdowns required to avoid serious and immediate risk of
equipment failure as force majeure.
40. State Commission Order dated 27.03.2015, referred by Appellant pertains
to True up of FY 2013-14 and it has been observed by State Commission, that
that low PLF for RGTPS unit 1 & 2 during FY 2013-14 and FY 2014-15 were not
in control of petitioner and petitioner has made sincere efforts to bring back the
machines in service in minimum possible time. However, our attention has been
drawn by Respondent that though State Commission appreciated the efforts of
Appellant, yet for the FY 2013-14, no relaxation in plant Availability factor was
granted for RGTPS. We refrain from making any observations on the said order
dated 27.03.2015 as it is not under challenge before us, however it is clear that
in spite of such favorable observation, no relaxation in PLF was granted for the
FY 2013-14 . Moreover, it is informed that for FY 2013-14, the low PLF arose
due to same circumstances i.e Rotar failure, like for the FY 2014-15, Appellant
chose not to challenge the order dated 27.03.2015 and same has attained finality
as far as FY 2013-14 is concerned for identical circumstances.
41. Our attention has also been drawn towards State Commission’s Order
dated 29.03.2013, in case No HERC /PRO -25 of 2012 for approval of Generation
tariff of HPGCL for the FY 2013-14, in which it is observed that RGTPS has been
able to achieve low PLF ( 27.65 % for Unit 1 and 75.84 % for unit 2) during FY
2012-13, Appellant itself has initially proposed a PLF of 80% for FY 2013-14 for
these plants, which was subsequently revised to 70 %. However, State
Commission in the said order considered the PLF of 70 % only for the purpose of
Page 21 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
working out target generation, while keeping the PLF at 85 % for full recovery of
fixed cost.
42. Therefore, there is no substance/merit in the contention of Appellant with
regard to violation of doctrine of legitimate expectation and principles of
regulatory consistency based on observation of State Commission in the order
dated 27.03.2015.
43. Appellant has relied upon Regulation 3.23 (vi)to contend that outage of
RGTPS unit in FY 2014-15 would fall in the category of Force Majeure which
reads as “ any shut down or interruptions, which is required to avoid serious and
immediate risks of a significant plant or equipment failure”. It is however
observed from the order dated 27.03.2015 passed by State Commission in
Petition No HERC/PRO-61 of 2014 for True up of FY 2013-14, that RGTPS (1&2)
plant has achieved low PLF since commissioning; 52.73 % ( FY 2011-12 ); 47.50
% ( FY 2013-14); 41.69 % ( FY 2013-14) and no documentary evidence has been
placed by Appellant if any relaxation was granted to RGTPS in these years. As
such these PLF figures for RGTPS plant since commissioning do establish, that
these units have been facing low PLF since commissioning on several accounts
like machine issue, coal supply and quality of coal and low PLF in FY 2014-15
does not seem to be an exception. Furthermore, the outage during the period
under consideration is on account of machine issue that these plants are facing
since commissioning.
44. It is a settled principle that the responsibility for procurement of quality
equipment, whether sourced domestically or imported, rests squarely upon the
generating company. The generating company having undertaken to establish
and operate the generating station, assumes the obligation to ensure that
Page 22 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
machinery and components are of requisite quality, fit for purpose, and
maintained in accordance with prudent utility practices. The Regulations
contemplate plant availability as a controllable parameter, and the generator
cannot shift the burden of equipment failure onto consumers or the regulatory
framework. The choice of supplier, whether indigenous or foreign, is a commercial
decision of the generator, and the attendant risks of quality, reliability, and timely
replacement are to be borne by it. Unless the failure is demonstrably attributable
to external uncontrollable causes, the generator remains accountable for
ensuring uninterrupted availability through procurement of sound equipment and
diligent upkeep thereof.
45. Accordingly, we do not find merit in the contention that the rotor damage of
an imported machine, resulting in reduced Plant Load Factor, can be brought
within the ambit of force majeure. The doctrine of force majeure is confined to
events beyond the reasonable control of the generating company, such as natural
calamities, war, or governmental prohibitions, and cannot be extended to cover
equipment breakdowns which fall within the realm of operational risk. Plant
availability is a controllable parameter under the Regulations, and outages arising
from machinery failure are ordinarily attributable to the generator’s maintenance
and operational responsibilities. Only where the inability to repair or replace the
rotor is demonstrably occasioned by external and uncontrollable causes—such
as statutory embargo on imports or global disruptions preventing supply of critical
spares—could the plea of force majeure be entertained. In the present case, in
the absence of such circumstances, the shortfall in PLF is to be treated as a
controllable event, and the generator cannot claim exemption under force
majeure.
Page 23 of 25

Judgement in Appeal No. 306 of 2016
46. With regard to the relaxation granted to WYC Hydel, the situation of RGTPS
and WYC is very different. It has been observed by the State Commission that
the WYC Hydel machine have outlived their useful life and the efficiency has gone
down considerably accordingly State Commission determined the PLF at 50%
for WYC Hydel for FY 2015-16, moreover such a decision has not been assailed
before us. As such, these observations did not amount to a general relaxation of
fixed charge recovery norms. Impugned Order need no interference on the issue
and we accordingly upheld the findings in the Impugned Order on the issue.
CONCLUSION
Our Views on both the issues are summarized as under:
ISSUE I: DIRECTION TO REFUND FIXED COSTS FOR PLANTS LESS THAN
10 YEARS.
Findings in the Impugned Order that annual fixed charges are to be calculated as
per Regulation 30(a) for RGTPP Units 1 & 2 and DCRTPP, which have not
completed ten years of commercial operation, are set aside. It is held that monthly
and annual fixed charges for these plants shall be calculated in terms of
Regulation 30(c)(i). The matter is accordingly remanded to the State Commission
to work out the annual fixed charges for these plants in the above terms.
ISSUE II: TRUING-UP OF FIXED COSTS WITHOUT CONSIDERING FORCE
MAJEURE CONDITIONS.
Page 24 of 25

Impugned Order need no interference on the issue and we accordingly uphold
the findings in the Impugned Order on the issue.

1. The present batch of appeals has been filed by Torrent Power Limited (“the
Appellant/TPL”), assailing the Tariff Orders dated 31.03.2020 (“impugned
orders”) as well as the order dated 12.05.2025 passed in Review Petition
(“Impugned Review Order”) by Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission

(hereinafter referred to as “State Commission/GERC”) for the Truing-Up for FY
2018-19 and determination of Tariff for FY 2020-21 for their three licensed area
of supply within the State of Gujarat, details whereof are set out below:

2. Since, the issues involved in above said impugned orders are similar and
arise out of identical factual and legal circumstances regarding the regulatory
treatment of uncovered FPPPA revenue and the denial of carrying cost, the
present batch of Appeals is being adjudicated and disposed of by way of this

DESCRIPTION OF PARTIES:
3. The Appellant herein, the Torrent Power Limited (“TPL”) is a Company
formed under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956 and is in the business
of generation, transmission and distribution of electricity.
4. The Respondent No. 1 is the Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission
(hereinafter referred as “State Commission/GERC”), established under the
provisions of the repealed Electricity Regulatory Commission Act, 1998 and so
continued in office, by virtue of Section 82 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (“the Act”).
FACTUAL MATRIX OF THE CASE: -
5. Appellant filed Petitions before the State Commission for the True-up of FY
2018-19 and for determination of tariff for its distribution business for supply of

electricity for the FY 2020-21 for the abovementioned circles in the State of
Gujarat.
6. On 31.03.2020, the Respondent Commission, passed the impugned orders
for the True-up of FY 2018-19 and for determination of tariff for the F.Y. 2020-21
for all the three circles separately. Subsequently, the Appellant filed Petitions
seeking Rectification cum Review of the order dated 31.03.2020 before the State
Commission, inter alia, raising the following issues:
i. Actual cost of generation of TPL-G considered instead of cost of scheduled
generation of TPL-D towards power purchase cost.
ii. Ignoring wheeling losses of LT Consumers.
iii. Failure to compute cross subsidy surcharge for high tension maximum
demand of metro rail.
iv. Inconsistency in directions issued regarding fuel and power purchase cost
adjustment (FPPCA).
v. Error in consideration of provisional revenue to compute revenue
gap/surplus.
vi. Failure to segregate recovery of earlier years approved gap/surplus.
7. Vide order dated 12.05.2025, State Commission partly allowed the Review
Petition; however, the claim pertaining to carrying cost was disallowed. Aggrieved
by the findings and conclusions recorded in the Impugned Orders, the Appellant
filed the present batch of appeals.
ANALYSIS & DISCUSSION:-
8. Appellant has raised following two issues, which are common in all the three
appeals for the adjudication: -

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 475 of 2022, 476 of 2022 & 189 of 2023
(a) GERC erred in considering provisional revenue instead of actual revenue
while determining the Gap /(Surplus) for FY 2018–19 during the true-up
exercise.
(b) GERC erred in denying carrying cost on approved past-period gaps.
Heard Mr. Amit Kapur, Learned Counsel appearing on behalf of Appellant, Mr.
Sitesh Mukherjee, Learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of Respondent
No.1 on the above issues, perused Impugned Orders, Written Submissions filed
by the parties and other documents placed on record. The issues are deliberated
below:
ISSUE A: Consideration of provisional revenue instead of Accrual
Revenue while determining Gap/surplus during True up of FY 2018-19
9. It is submitted on behalf of Appellant that subsequent to adoption of Ind AS-
115 for the year FY 2018-19, TPL was required to recognize
provisional/unrecovered revenue on an accrual basis in its books of accounts
corresponding to all approved and legitimate expenses which are yet to be
approved by commission and even yet to be recovered from consumers.
However, Appellant submitted revenue gap for FY 2018-19 on the basis of billed
revenue for all the three circles and this billed amount excludes the amount
specifically disclosed under Note 44. GERC in the Impugned Orders relied upon
Note 29 of the Audited Accounts, while completely ignoring Note 44, which
clarified the impact due to adoption of Ind AS 115. Details of billed revenue,
accrued revenue and approved Revenue as per Ind AS 115 in Impugned Orders
is submitted for FY 2018-19 for the three circles:

10. Learned Senior Counsel appearing on the behalf of State Commission does
not dispute that revenue has been considered in terms of Audited accounts
however, contended that Note 44 reveals that accrued revenue is entirely
attributable to FPPPA claims recognized during the final quarter (Q4) of FY 2018-
19 which were recognized only when billed to consumers. Pursuant to TPL's own
communication dated 30.04.2019, which confirmed the billing at the updated
FPPPA rate of Rs. 2.11 per kWh commencing from the billing month of April 2019
and therefore, in a rolling account, these amounts were physically received within
weeks of the fiscal year-end, and the underlying accrual gap was accordingly
liquidated. It is further submitted that the total audited eligible FPPPA rate was
Rs. 2.66 per unit. By billing at Rs. 2.11 per kWh, the TPL secured recovery of the
base cost along with its incremental cost pool from the very first month of the
subsequent financial year, rather than waiting for a two-year true-up cycle. Under
the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle of regulatory accounting, the initial revenue
collected in a new period automatically liquidates the oldest outstanding
operational deficits of the preceding period. The Rs. 37.86 Crore variance
(difference between actual audited FPPPA cost of Rs. 195.64 Crore and
provisional booking of Rs. 157.78 Crore for Q4 FY 2018-19) was completely
liquidated through the cash inflow of Rs. 195.64 Crore collected in Q1 of FY 2019-
20.

11. In response to the contention of State Commission, that FPPPA pertaining
to Q4 of FY 2018–19 was recovered in Q1 of FY 2019–20, and the accrued
FPPPA revenue had already been considered in FY 2018–19 itself, Appellant
relied upon the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Mohinder Singh Gill
v. Chief Election Commissioner & Anr., (1978) 1 SCC 405 to emphasize the
settled legal position that the GERC cannot supplement, improve, or sustain the
Impugned Order by advancing fresh reasons not contained therein. Without
prejudice to this contention, Appellant vide its affidavit dated 05.05.2026
submitted quarterly FPPPA details for FY 2017-18, 2018-19, and 2019-20 to
demonstrate that the FPPPA revenue pertaining to Q4 of a financial year was
consistently treated as part of billed revenue on a provisional basis in the same
financial year; the differential between provisional Q4 booking and actual Q1
recovery was treated as FPPPA revenue of the succeeding year. Such
methodology was consistently followed even prior to adoption of Ind AS-115 and
the same is recorded in Note 41/44 of the Respective Accounts. Specifically, the
differential amounts of Rs. 37.86 Crore in respect of Surat (Appeal No. 475 of
2022), Rs. 2.35 Crore in respect of Dahej (Appeal No. 476 of 2022), and Rs.
147.79 Crore in respect of Ahmedabad-Gandhinagar (Appeal No. 189 of 2023).
In each case, the said differential formed part of the total FPPPA revenue — being
Rs. 685.81 Crore (Surat), Rs. 62.28 Crore (Dahej), and Rs. 1,621.73 Crore
(Ahmedabad-Gandhinagar) — reflected in Form-10 of the respective Truing-up
Petitions for FY 2019-20 as part of total revenues of Rs. 2,326.15 Crore, Rs.
239.87 Crore, and Rs. 5,729.75 Crore respectively, which were subsequently
approved by GERC as revenue from 'Sale of Power' for FY 2019-20 at Paragraph
4.7.12 of the Truing-up Order (Surat and Ahmedabad-Gandhinagar) and
Paragraph 4.6.11 of the Truing-up Order (Dahej). It is, therefore, submitted that
the same differential amounts cannot again be attributed to FY 2018-19 under
Page 9 of 24

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 475 of 2022, 476 of 2022 & 189 of 2023
GERC's FIFO theory, since they already stand accounted for and approved as
revenue for FY 2019-20 — a re-attribution would result in an impermissible
duplication and double counting of revenue across all three licensed areas of
supply.
12. The reliance placed by Appellant upon Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief
Election Commissioner & Anr., (1978) 1 SCC 405, to confine the Appellate
Tribunal to only the recorded reasoning of the Regulatory Commission is
misplaced. The dictum in Mohinder Singh Gill was rendered in the context of
administrative orders, where supplementation of reasons post facto would
undermine transparency and accountability. In the said judgement, the Supreme
Court left it to the Election Tribunal (i.e. the High Court hearing the Election
Petition filed by the Respondent) to examine the election petition on its merits.
Accepting the contention of Appellant would mean that this Tribunal would be
required, after setting aside the impugned tariff order, to remand the matter to the
Commission to pass an order afresh assigning reasons. The appellate
jurisdiction conferred upon this Tribunal under Section 111 of the Electricity Act,
2003, is distinct and wider in scope. As the first appellate forum, APTEL is
mandated to examine the legality, propriety and correctness of the impugned
order on both facts and law based on the entire record of proceedings before the
Commission. A first appeal is a rehearing of the original proceedings, and the
appellate forum possesses all powers, jurisdiction and authority as the forum of
first instance, the jurisdiction and range of subjects being co-extensive
(“Southern Power Distribution Company of AP Limited v. Andhra Pradesh
Electricity Regulatory Commission, 2022 SCC OnLine APTEL 110; H-Energy
(P) Ltd. v. Petroleum & Natural Gas Regulatory Board, 2023 SCC OnLine
APTEL 17). In the present case, we shall accordingly proceed to decide the issue
on its merit.
Page 10 of 24

Judgement in Appeal Nos. 475 of 2022, 476 of 2022 & 189 of 2023
13. We note from the details submitted by TPL vide its respective affidavit dated
01.05.2026, the billing details for FY 2018-19 and FY 2019-20 for all the three
circles. For example, for Surat (Appeal 475 of 2022), the billed revenue as
submitted in Form 10 of the Petition is indicated as Rs. 2279.66 Crore, while the
total revenue as per Ind AS 115 (Note 29) is Rs 2322.92 Crore, which has been
considered in the Impugned Order for working out the gap/surplus. It is also
observed from Note 44 that “Consequent to adoption of Ind AS 115, Revenue
from Operations and Profit for the year ended 31st march 2019 are higher by Rs
43.26 Crore”. It is to note from the review order dated 12.05.2025, that as TPL
has claimed total tax on the total revenue (Rs 2322.92 Crore) of Rs 14.75 Crore,
same was approved by the commission and approved the revenue from sale of
Power as Rs 2322.92 Crore. Likewise, the details are for other two circles.

30. Admittedly, carrying cost serves a very specific purpose in regulatory and
financial contexts: the doctrine of awarding ‘carrying cost’ as bona fide
compensation for the “time value of money” and therefore, must be given for the
deprivation of the monies, when expenditure or revenue recovery is deferred. It
is a settled legal principle (“Punjab State Power Corporation v. PSERC; 2022
SCC ONLine APTEL 46”; Reliance Infrastructure Ltd. v. MERC, 2012 SCC
OnLine APTEL 154;) that where recovery of legitimate expenditure is deferred,
the affected utility is entitled to carrying cost on the unrecovered sum. The
rationale lies in the recognition of the time value of money and the financing
burden borne by the utility during the period of non-recovery. The imposition of
carrying cost ensures that the utility is placed in the same financial position as it
would have been had timely recovery been permitted, thereby neutralizing the
adverse impact of regulatory delay. Accordingly, the amount withheld from
recovery need to be restituted with carrying cost at the rate determined under the
applicable Regulations, so as to secure equity between the utility and the
consumers and to uphold the integrity of the tariff determination process.
31. We find considerable merit in the submissions advanced on behalf of the
Appellant that once a tariff order is modified pursuant to review or appellate
proceedings, the doctrine of merger operates, whereby the modification does not
remain a separate or collateral determination but becomes an integral part of the
original tariff order itself. The consequence of such merger is that the amounts so
approved or quantified in appellate adjudication necessarily form part of the
approved past period gaps and, in turn, constitute the opening gap for the
purpose of computation of carrying cost in subsequent regulatory exercises. It is,

of regulatory parity requires that the time value of money be preserved, and any
regulatory lag neutralized, by allowing carrying cost on such sums from the date
they became due until their eventual adjustment.
32. In the present case, Regulation 21.6 of the GERC MYT Regulations, 2016,
assumes significance as extracted below:
“c) Carrying cost to be allowed on the amount of Revenue Gap
or Revenue Surplus for the period from the date on which such
gap/surplus has become due, i.e., from the end of the year for
which true-up has been done, till the end of the year in which
it is addressed, calculated on simple interest basis at the
weighted average State Bank Base Rate for the relevant year,
i.e., the year for which Revenue Gap or Revenue Surplus is
determined:
Provided that carrying cost on the amount of Revenue Gap
shall be allowed up to the above limit, subject to prudence
check and submission of documentary evidence for having
incurred the carrying cost in the years prior to the year in which
the revenue gap is addressed;”
33. The Regulation explicitly and deliberately prescribes that carrying cost shall
be calculated on simple interest basis at the weighted average State Bank Base
Rate for the relevant year. The deliberate use of the adjective "simple" is a
conscious legislative choice and, in terms of the principle of expressio unius est
exclusio alterius, the express specification of simple interest operates as an
equally express exclusion of compound interest. This principle was affirmed by
the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State of Haryana v. S.L. Arora & Co. (2010) 3
SCC 690., wherein it was held that Compound Interest can be awarded only if
there is a specific contract or authority under a statute, for compounding of

Ltd. V. General Electric Co.; 1994 Supp.(1) SCC 644, where it was held that
interest on interest was not opposed to the public policy of India, but could ne
awarded only if authorised by the contract or statute. Accordingly, as the mode
of computation is statutorily fixed and therefore, this Tribunal can only accord
simple interest where the governing Regulation has made the choice explicit.
34. Hon'ble Supreme Court in Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Adani
Power (Mundra) Ltd. (2023) 2 SCC 624 and GMR Warora Energy Ltd. v. CERC
(2023) 10 SCC 401 upheld the grant of compound interest on carrying cost in the
context of change-in-law events under PPAs, those decisions operated in a
contractual and restitutionary framework where no express regulatory
prescription governed the mode of interest. The present case is materially
distinguishable — Regulation 21.6(c) expressly occupies the field and prescribes
simple interest as the applicable mode. Where the subordinate legislation has
made an explicit provision, equitable or restitutionary principles cannot be
invoked to override or supplement the statutory mandate.

adjudication merge with the original tariff order, form part of the approved past
period gaps, and necessarily attract carrying cost from the date they became due
until their eventual accounting in the ARR, in conformity with Regulation 21.6 of
the GERC MYT Regulations, 2016. Accordingly, the issue is remanded to State
Commission to work out the carrying cost, in all the three appeals in terms of
Regulations on the amount so quantified during FY 2018-19, true up stage, on
which the carrying cost was not considered by the State Commission in the ARR
for FY 2020-21.
